sections.text: तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्स्वबान्धवान्। स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव
Therefore, we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our relatives; for how can we be happy by killing our own people, O Madhava (Krishna)?
यद्यप्येते न पश्यन्ति लोभोपहतचेतसः। कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं मित्रद्रोहे च पातकम्
Though they, with intelligence overpowered by greed, see no evil in the destruction of families, and no sin in hostility to friends,
कथं न ज्ञेयमस्माभिः पापादस्मान्निवर्तितुम्। कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं प्रपश्यद्भिर्जनार्दन
Why should not we who clearly see evil in the destruction of families, learn to turn away from this sin, O Janardana (Krishna)?

These three verses capture one of the most psychologically acute moments in the entire Gita. Arjuna has moved from describing the horror of what hes about to do to making what seems like a perfectly reasonable moral argument. And this is where things get interesting.
Look at the progression of his thinking: In verse 37, he appeals to Krishna as Madhava, a name that emphasizes Krishnas divine nature. Hes essentially saying, Youre the Supreme Lord. Surely you understand that killing ones own people cannot lead to happiness. Its a clever move. Hes not just expressing despair anymore; hes constructing an argument.
And then comes verse 38, where Arjuna reveals something fascinating about how he sees his opponents. He says that they, Duryodhana and his party, are blinded by greed. Their minds are clouded. They cannot see the sin theyre committing by destroying families and betraying friends. In other words, they have an excuse: ignorance.
But verse 39 delivers the real punch. Arjuna says: We can see clearly. We understand exactly whats wrong with this situation. And precisely because we see clearly, we have a greater responsibility to turn away from this sin.
This is where Arjunas argument becomes both compelling and problematic.
On the surface, it makes perfect sense. If I know something is wrong and do it anyway, am I not more culpable than someone who acts from ignorance? Isnt knowledge supposed to guide action? Isnt the wise person supposed to refrain from harmful acts?
Yes, and yet.
Arjuna is using valid spiritual principles to arrive at an invalid conclusion. This is one of the minds most sophisticated tricks: using dharma to justify adharma, using wisdom to rationalize avoidance, using compassion as a mask for fear.
The key word in verse 38 is lobha, greed. Arjuna accuses his enemies of being driven by greed. But wait. What is driving Arjuna right now? Is it pure moral clarity? Or is it something else wearing the clothes of moral clarity?
Consider: Arjuna doesnt want to lose his loved ones. He doesnt want to bear the psychological burden of having killed his grandfather, his teacher, his cousins. He doesnt want to live with that memory. These are understandable human desires. But they are, in their own way, also forms of attachment, of wanting things to be a certain way, of grasping at a particular outcome.
The Gita will spend the next seventeen chapters addressing exactly this confusion. For now, we simply need to notice it.
Theres another layer to explore here. Arjuna says he can clearly see the evil of destroying families. But seeing clearly is precisely what hes not doing.
Heres what Arjuna is not seeing: Hes not seeing that this war has been coming for decades. Hes not seeing that every peaceful option was exhausted. Hes not seeing that Duryodhana rejected every compromise, every appeal to justice, every opportunity for reconciliation. Hes not seeing that sometimes standing up to adharma requires actions that are painful.
Most importantly, hes not seeing himself clearly. He thinks hes being noble. He thinks refusing to fight is the ethical choice. But mixed into his reasoning are threads of fear, attachment, and confusion that he cant distinguish from his genuine moral concerns.
This is the human condition. We rarely have pure motives. Our noblest intentions are intertwined with our fears and desires. The person who refuses to have a difficult conversation to keep the peace may genuinely care about peace, and may also be afraid of conflict. The person who doesnt want to hurt anyone may be compassionate, and may also be avoiding the discomfort of standing firm.
Arjuna is not a villain. Hes not being dishonest. He is genuinely confused. And thats the point. The Gita takes seriously the fact that confusion can feel like clarity, that attachment can dress itself up as wisdom.
Theres a beautiful irony in verse 39 that often goes unnoticed. Arjuna asks: Why should we not learn to turn away from this sin?
Learn. He uses the word jñeya, that which should be known, that which should be learned.
But learning is exactly whats about to happen. Krishna is going to teach him. The next seventeen chapters are Arjunas education. And what will he learn? Not that killing is good. Not that compassion doesnt matter. But that his understanding of the situation is incomplete, that his identification of what constitutes sin and virtue is confused, that his notion of who he is and what hes doing needs to be fundamentally revised.
The great teaching is coming. But it can only come because Arjuna asked for it, even though he didnt know he was asking. His anguish, his paralysis, his philosophical objections, all of these created the opening through which wisdom could enter.
In verse 7 of Chapter 2, Arjuna will formally ask Krishna to teach him. But in a sense, the request is already implicit here. A mind that is questioning, struggling, refusing to act from blind obedience, this is a mind that is ready to learn.
Lets also notice how Arjuna addresses Krishna in these verses. In verse 37, he says Madhava, emphasizing Krishnas divine descent through the Madhu lineage. In verse 39, he says Janardana, a name meaning one who causes people to tremble or more positively one who answers the prayers of people.
These names reveal something about Arjunas state. Hes appealing to Krishnas divinity, his power, his role as the one who responds to devotees prayers. On some level, Arjuna knows that what he needs right now is not just practical advice but divine guidance. He may think he wants Krishna to validate his choice not to fight. But deeper down, hes calling out to the divine for rescue from his own confusion.
Every sincere prayer is like this. We think we know what we want. We think were asking for something specific. But underneath the specific request is a more fundamental cry: Help me. Show me. I am lost.
These verses also touch on one of lifes most difficult truths: the fact that others wrongdoing does not excuse us from our own responsibilities.
Arjuna says, in effect: They are blinded by greed. They dont see clearly. Therefore they can be excused for their actions. But we see clearly, so we should act accordingly.
The logic seems impeccable. But heres the problem: In a world where everyone excused themselves from difficult action by pointing to others moral failures, nothing would ever get done. Evil would flourish unchecked, protected by the scruples of good people who didnt want to dirty their hands.
This is one of the oldest moral debates in human history. How do we respond to wrongdoing? Is it better to remain pure and let evil triumph? Or to engage with the messy, morally ambiguous work of opposing it?
The Gitas answer will be nuanced. It wont simply say fight or dont fight. It will reframe the entire question by introducing the concept of nishkama karma, action without attachment to results. It will distinguish between the action itself and the ego that claims ownership of the action. It will show that the real sin is not in acting but in acting from a place of ego, attachment, and delusion.
But were not there yet. Right now, were sitting with Arjuna in his confusion. And perhaps thats where we need to start, acknowledging our own confusion, our own mixed motives, our own sophisticated rationalizations. Before we can receive the teaching, we have to feel the weight of not knowing.
Theres something else worth exploring in these verses, the concept of sukha, happiness. In verse 37, Arjuna asks: How can we be happy by killing our own people?
Its a reasonable question. And it points to something fundamental about how most of us think about ethics and action. We tend to evaluate our choices based on whether they will make us happy or unhappy. Will this bring me peace? Will I be able to live with myself?
But the Gita is going to challenge this entire framework. Krishna will eventually teach that true happiness, ananda, doesnt depend on external circumstances at all. It doesnt come from the results of our actions, whether pleasant or painful. It comes from something deeper, something that remains constant regardless of what happens in the world.
Arjuna is worried about his future mental state. Hes trying to protect his peace of mind. And from one perspective, this seems wise. But from another perspective, it reveals the problem: hes making his decision based on attachment to a particular inner state rather than based on what the situation actually requires.
This is subtle, and its worth sitting with. We often pride ourselves on being conscientious people who care about the consequences of our actions. But sometimes that very conscientiousness becomes another form of self-centeredness, were so focused on how well feel afterward that we cant see clearly what needs to be done now.
The word kula appears repeatedly in these verses, it means family, lineage, or clan. Arjuna speaks of kulakshaya, the destruction of families. This was a profound concern in the ancient world, where family lineage carried tremendous weight, where ancestral traditions were passed down through generations, where the continuity of the clan was seen as sacred.
But heres the thing: the Kauravas had already destroyed the family. Duryodhanas greed, his jealousy, his repeated attempts to murder his cousins, his public humiliation of Draupadi, all of this had already torn the fabric of the family apart. The war wasnt destroying something intact; it was the final consequence of decades of destruction that had already occurred.
Arjuna speaks as if he has a choice between preserving the family and destroying it. But that choice was made long ago, by others. What Arjuna actually faces is a different choice: whether to stand up for dharma in the aftermath of destruction, or to let adharma triumph unchallenged.
This distinction matters in our own lives too. We sometimes imagine that by withdrawing from conflict, were preserving peace. But often, by the time we face a difficult choice, the damage has already been done by others. Our choice isnt between peace and conflict; its between facing reality and pretending it doesnt exist.
One final observation about these verses. Notice that Arjuna is still talking. Hes been making arguments for verses now, philosophical, emotional, moral arguments. Hes been eloquent. Hes been passionate. Hes made some excellent points.
But he hasnt asked Krishna for guidance yet. Not really. Hes presenting his case, building his argument, trying to convince Krishna that hes right. Hes still operating from the assumption that he understands the situation and just needs validation.
The real breakthrough will come in Chapter 2, when Arjuna finally admits: I dont know whats right. Im confused. Please teach me. Until he reaches that point of genuine not-knowing, no teaching can enter.
This is true for all of us. As long as were sure were right, as long as were building our case and making our arguments, were not actually open to learning anything new. Wisdom requires a particular kind of humility, the willingness to admit that our current understanding might be incomplete or mistaken.
Arjuna isnt there yet. But hes getting closer. Each verse brings him nearer to the point of surrender. And thats the arc of Chapter 1: the gradual dissolution of certainty, the slow crumbling of confidence, until finally theres enough openness for something new to emerge.

In verse 37, Arjuna delivers what seems like a moral conclusion: Tasmat na arha vayam hantum, THEREFORE we should not kill Dhritarashtras sons, our relatives. Notice the word tasmat, therefore. Hes concluded his argument. But verse 38 reveals the subtle trick his mind is playing: Yadyapi ete na pashyanti lobhopahatachetasah, though THEY, with minds overpowered by greed (lobha), do not see the evil in destroying families. In other words: they have an excuse, theyre blinded by greed. But we see clearly! Verse 39 completes the trap: Katham na jneyam asmabhih papad asman nivartitum, why should WE not know to turn away from this sin, we who clearly see the evil? This is one of the minds most sophisticated tricks: using dharma to justify adharma, using wisdom to rationalize avoidance. Theyre ignorant; were wise; therefore, we should act differently. It sounds noble. But examine it closely. Arjuna is using valid spiritual principles to reach an invalid conclusion. Yes, knowledge brings greater responsibility. Yes, we should not act from greed. But Arjunas clarity is itself a form of not-seeing. Hes not seeing the thirteen years of injustice. Hes not seeing that every peaceful option was exhausted. Hes not seeing that sometimes opposing adharma requires difficult action. Reflect on where youve elevated yourself morally to justify inaction: I wont stoop to their level, Im above this conflict, Someone of my values doesnt engage in such things. Sometimes these are genuine wisdom. Sometimes theyre fear dressed in spiritual clothing. The Gita will teach us to tell the difference, but first, we must be honest enough to question our own clarity.
